beats.say: The caret is between the parentheses for the cat’s left eye. An empty pair draws an open eye. Send a request for a completion in those parentheses. While it travels, move the caret down to the right eye.
The reply arrives for the left eye. It offers the word shut, in quotes. The file still has the same two lines. No second request went out. If you press Tab now, which eye should close?

Neither eye closes. Look at the two empty calls. Moving the caret changed where the developer was working. The editor discarded the late reply before it could appear as a suggestion. Follow the next edit from the local lookup to the text that survives on the page.

In the permission helper, type Polic. The import already contains the rest of PolicyGraph. A local prefix index can finish the name. After graph dot, the editor knows the receiver’s type. Where can it find the method called allows?

The language server lists that method from the type. This exact lookup works locally when the index is ready. If type information is missing, look for a lexical match or use a permitted remote candidate. Try a dedented line below a function. A backward scan finds its header, but the caret is outside that function. Use syntax-node ranges to recover the enclosing scope, including when the current line is incomplete.

Now stop at the empty assignment. The return below it needs a value. The client checks whether this buffer may leave the laptop. With permission, a bounded model request can suggest an expression using the surrounding code. The gateway independently checks access and upload policy on remote requests. If upload is denied, the client keeps this buffer on the device. Predicting the next edit elsewhere, or planning and testing a multi-file patch, belongs to a different interaction and time budget.

Return to the permitted helper. At the empty assignment, a single-line expression will do. In this scenario, stop at the line ending or twenty-four output tokens, whichever comes first. Aim for two hundred milliseconds at p ninety-five. Measure from the edit to the first usable paint. After the function signature, the developer still needs a whole body. This candidate computes the value on one line and returns it on the next. Stop at the end of the body or ninety-six output tokens, with a five-hundred-millisecond p ninety-five target. Measure that class separately so slower body completions stay visible.

Take the permitted single-line request for this helper. The client can send the two sides of the assignment to the decoder. The gap begins just after the equals sign and its space. Read below it. The newline and return statement are already in the file. A prefix-only model would miss that constraint.

Copy the prefix from the start of the body to the caret. Copy the suffix from the caret to the end. This checkpoint expects a prefix marker, the prefix, a suffix marker, the suffix, and a middle marker. During fill-in-the-middle training, the missing span follows those two boundaries. A left-to-right decoder can now predict it.
The decoder offers graph dot allows, called with request. Which part comes back to the file?

Insert the middle. The original newline still leads to exactly one return. The labels on the prompt stand for this checkpoint’s trained sentinel tokens. Encode source as ordinary content. A plausible call still needs the real method signature and a test of the permission rule.

title: Where does the suffix actually begin?

beats.say: Try a smaller file. There is an a, a smiling face, and a b. Put the caret immediately after the face. The editor reports three UTF-sixteen units before it. A Python service will slice this string. What must survive on the right?

Keep the b. The face takes two UTF-sixteen units, four UTF-eight bytes, and one Python code point. Count from the start of the line. The same boundary is three units in the editor, five bytes, or Python index two. Copying three into the Python slice loses the b. Convert on the captured document before building the prompt.

title: How much of the next snippet fits?

beats.say: Build an eight-thousand-token input for this example. Authorize the files before ranking them. A private match stays out even if it shares every symbol. Among permitted files, shared imports and definitions can help rank the code that explains the method call. For example, a permitted file shares two symbols out of four in the union. Its overlap score is one half. The denied file never enters that comparison.

Reserve two hundred tokens for framing and a thousand for the suffix. Add forty-five hundred prefix tokens and eighteen hundred for permitted definitions. Another permitted snippet offers nine hundred tokens. How much can you take while keeping the return?

Take five hundred. The input is full. The return keeps its entire allocation. Reserve output capacity separately within the model’s total context window. Extra input also takes time to transfer and prefill, so compare context policies under the actual latency and privacy requirements.

title: Can this buffer cross the boundary?

beats.say: Upload permission is only the first check. Here a permitted source file contains a fictional token that the local scanner recognizes. Mask the token in a copy before upload. The mapping stays on the laptop. A returned placeholder stays visible for human review.
Try another buffer with the same token and an existing placeholder. The scanner reserves that prefix for its own replacements. Can it safely send a masked copy under this rule?

Keep the whole buffer local. A collision could make the mapping ambiguous. The source stays intact in both cases. A pattern scanner only catches known forms. Enforce tenant identity and retention rules at the gateway. Allowlist telemetry fields and check logs and caches, including in a private deployment. Return to the first masked copy, which the gateway received for inference. This enterprise configuration turns off raw prompt collection. By default it also disables training export. That permission covers the inference request alone.

Back at the right eye, capture the file, version, selection, policy and request counter together. Send a fresh request. When the reply matches, paint its word in pale ink. Both eyes stay open while the letters are only a preview.
Leave the caret there and change the upload policy. The buffer version is still eight. Which word can Tab insert now?

Tab inserts nothing. The policy change cleared the ghost immediately and advanced the counter. At acceptance, compare again and apply the saved range in one editor transaction. An edit, selection move or policy change invalidates pending work even when it sends no new request. Propagate cancellation to save compute. If an older reply finishes last, discard it and preserve any newer fresh ghost.

title: How long did the developer wait?

beats.say: Time the permitted single-line expression. Start a clock at the qualifying edit. This invented serial path spends twelve milliseconds on client handling, fifty-five on transport, twenty-eight on context, seventy-eight in the queue and model through a usable span, and ten checking and painting it. Stop at fresh paint. That totals one hundred eighty-three milliseconds, seventeen inside the two-hundred-millisecond objective.
Ordinary typing waits a hundred fifty milliseconds before submitting. This debounce lets the next letter cancel the timer. Keep all five stages the same. Where does the second trace end?

At three hundred thirty-three milliseconds. The wait crosses the objective before the developer sees the suggestion. Shorten the debounce, choose a local route, or specify a separate pause-to-paint objective. Request submission to the first token measures a different interval inside the path. Adding it again would count time twice.

title: Which requests make up the tail?

beats.say: A worksheet gives you a budget. A measured ninety-fifth percentile needs complete traces. In this invented batch, one request spends a hundred milliseconds in stage A, and a different request spends a hundred in stage B. Each other stage takes one millisecond. Trace both slow rows from start to finish.
Sort the twenty request totals. Nearest-rank p ninety-five selects the nineteenth entry. What time does that developer experience?

One hundred one milliseconds. Eighteen requests finish in two. The slow requests occupy both final positions. Each stage on its own has nineteen fast observations, so adding the two stage percentiles gives only two milliseconds. Report stale drops, errors and timeouts alongside completed latencies. Filtering down to painted successes can hide a broken service.

title: When does the warm worker win?

beats.say: Two eligible workers can produce this suggestion. In this timing example, both get the same twelve-hundred-token header and eighty new tokens. Cold prefill costs seventy-two milliseconds. On the warm worker, matching key and value blocks leave eleven milliseconds of prefill. Each worker still spends twenty-four milliseconds decoding the output. Compare service alone.
Cold takes ninety-six milliseconds and warm takes thirty-five. Now put seventy milliseconds of extra queueing on the warm worker. With all other waits equal, which one finishes earlier?

Choose cold. The warm route now takes one hundred five milliseconds. Cache affinity saves sixty-one milliseconds of prefill, less than the extra wait. Reuse only whole matching token blocks under the same authenticated scope, model, adapter and tokenizer configuration. An early token edit invalidates dependent blocks from that point on. A different tenant starts cold. Every result still goes through the editor’s freshness check.

title: How can a draft keep the target distribution?

beats.say: Prefill reads the input. Speculative decoding works on the output. A cheap draft proposes several tokens and the target checks them together. In this example it keeps four, then corrects the fifth. Five tokens come out. A full match may earn a bonus if generation can continue. Speed depends on draft cost, verification cost and the other requests sharing the batch.

Zoom in on one stochastic choice with the same three tokens in both models. The draft picked A with probability point five. The target gives A point two. Accept with the smaller of one and the target probability divided by the draft probability. What fraction of these proposals survives?

Two fifths survive. On rejection, subtract draft from target in every column and keep the positive differences. B lacks point one and C lacks point two. Normalize that missing mass of point three. B gets one third and C gets two thirds. Sampling the correction this way restores the target distribution. Check equivalence and measure edit-to-paint tails by language and suggestion type before enabling speculation.

title: How many tokens need new prefill each second?

beats.say: Scale that request to five thousand active editors. At point four requests per second each, two thousand requests arrive every second. Sixty percent cancel before GPU admission. Eight hundred survive. A later cancellation can still spend GPU time.

Split the survivors evenly. Their average prompt length is two thousand forty-eight tokens. Incoming volume counts every prompt token, including the cached ones. To find new prefill work, multiply within each group. Each hit carries three thousand seventy-two tokens and skips three quarters of its prefill. Each miss carries one thousand twenty-four tokens and needs them all. The two contributions sum to seven hundred sixteen thousand eight hundred newly prefilled tokens per second. That is the work left after cache reuse.
Swap the two prompt lengths. Keep the hit rate and the overall mean fixed. Does the prefill load stay the same?

The long requests now miss. Their entire length must be read. Total work rises to one million three hundred thirty-one thousand two hundred newly prefilled tokens per second. At twenty thousand effective prefill tokens per GPU-second, the worksheet grows from thirty-six GPUs to sixty-seven. Decode, late cancellations, memory, failures and headroom still need a mixed-load measurement.

Watch two slots on one worker. At the end of step eight, A has decoded two tokens. B has decoded six and needs more. C is waiting. The developer cancels A. That frees one slot while B is still running. Does C need to wait for B to finish?

The scheduler can admit C on step nine. C starts prefill with its own prompt while B decodes its next token using its existing state. At the end of this step, B has seven tokens and C is ready to decode its first. The requests share the resident weights. Measure queue time and edit-to-paint latency under that mix of arrivals, cancellations, prefill and decode. A busy GPU can still leave an editor waiting.

Watch suggestion A on the assignment line. The developer accepts all eighteen characters of graph dot allows, called with user. It becomes solid code. Now undo that one insertion. Watch the closing parenthesis and the counts beneath it.

The line is empty after the equals sign. A still counts as accepted, and zero of its original characters remain. In the same observation window, the developer accepts all four characters of B and keeps them. C inserts forty-two, then loses seven original characters. D appears and is dismissed. Count each shown suggestion once, even if the developer accepts it word by word.

Three of four shown IDs were accepted. Thirty-nine of sixty-four inserted characters survived. A replacement character earns no credit for the original. An unfinished observation window is censored. A retained permission error still needs a correctness test. Freeze the edit point for offline tests. In an online comparison, hold the trigger and display policy fixed and compare shown rate, retained edits, stale drops, latency and cost per useful edit by language and suggestion type.

Take suggestion B from the previous cohort. All four characters of True survived. Freeze the source and the two test requests at the edit point. This user may read the document. The same user may not write to it. Run both cases with the retained expression. Which test catches the mistake?

The write test fails. Returning True approves both requests. Try the policy method in this fixture. It checks the requested action against the allowed set. The read stays allowed and the write is denied. The four retained characters told us what the developer kept. These tests tell us how it behaves in these two cases.

Use the same held-out edit points when comparing a smaller or quantized model. Compressing weights can save memory. Suppose a smaller candidate returns True. Replay the same two requests against both expressions. Check syntax, behavior and any public-code matches that need provenance review. At rollout, measure edit-to-paint p ninety-five separately for single-line expressions and multiline bodies. Compare quality and failures within each class too. Keep a known-good route for a slice that regresses.

Try a fresh replay at version eight under policy one. Request twenty is for the right eye. While it travels, move up to the left eye and back down. A new request goes out from the same parentheses. The file, version, policy and range all match the old ones. The editor’s counter is now twenty-three.
The new reply arrives first. The old one arrives last. Both offer exactly the same quoted word. Which reply can Tab use, and what should the preview show until you press it?

Use reply twenty-three. It matches the live snapshot. Discarding twenty leaves the newer pale word in place. Press Tab. The checked insertion turns solid and only the right eye closes. That is a test you can run with the replies delivered in either order. The next capstone carries the same isolation and accounting rules onto a shared multi-tenant platform.
